children: By Jessica Fleetham

The huge amount of money companies are looking to borrow in bond markets to fund AI-related investment creates competition for governments and helps push government-bond yields higher, according to Banque Cantonale du Valais.

This upward pressure comes on top of concerns about fiscal spending and high levels of debt, as well as expectations that central banks will hike interest rates further due to high energy prices, the Swiss bank's heads of asset management and investment strategy said in an interview.

These factors have caused yields on some major government bonds to surge to multidecade highs. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield hit a peak of 5.160% on Thursday, its highest since July 2007, while the 10-year German Bund yield reached 3.605%, its highest since 2009, Tradeweb data showed. Japanese 10-year government-bond yields hit a 40-year high.

Large AI-related companies bought back shares a few years ago and now they are issuing significant amounts of bonds in global capital markets, which is adding a lot of pressure to government-bond yields, Gero Jung, head of investment strategy, said.

Total global corporate bond issuance by the five major hyperscalers--large technology companies which operate global data center infrastructure--Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle has reached $227.64 billion so far in 2026, LSEG data showed. Estimates of total AI-related debt issuance for full-year 2026 range from around $300 billion to $570 billion, according to a report by Vanguard last month.
"We have, not necessarily a new, but certainly a substantial actor that is using capital markets and bond markets in particular," Jung said.

With government-bond yields at such high levels, including the 10-year Treasury yield above 5% for the first time in many years, this could create issues for governments as it increases debt servicing costs, Daniel Farquet, head of asset management and advisory, said.
"And refinancing is getting a lot more expensive," Farquet added.

Banque Cantonale du Valais has held an underweight position in government bonds, including eurozone government bonds, "for some time," Jung said. However, one of the bank's biggest convictions is in eurozone high-yield corporate bonds.
"That's one of our largest bets," Jung said.
One of the reasons for this view is that the eurozone economy has performed surprisingly well recently, he said.
"We think Europe is pretty much resilient today and will remain so in the near future."

Evidence of this economic resilience came as Wednesday's composite purchasing managers' index for the eurozone, which measures activity in the region's services and manufacturing sector, rose more than expected to 53.1 in September from 52.0 in August to reach the highest level in almost three-and-a-half years.
Meanwhile, the significant rise in bond yields in Japan has potential implications for the Japanese yen, they said.

Japanese 10-year government bond yields trading above 3% will dent the yen's appeal as a funding currency in carry trades--where investors borrow in a low-yielding currency to invest in higher-yielding currencies elsewhere--particularly as the Bank of Japan is expected to raise interest rates further, Jung said.
This could help the Japanese yen to recover. The yen "is still extremely cheap," he said.
"It's got quite a lot of scope to rise."

The U.S. dollar hit a 40-year high of 163.98 yen in late July, LSEG data showed. Since then, the yen has recovered, but continues to trade at very weak levels. The dollar on Thursday hit a three-week high of 158.98 yen.

By contrast, the Swiss franc is increasingly popular for funding carry trades as hedge funds switch away from the yen, Farquet said. Swiss interest rates stand at zero, inflation in the country is low and the 10-year Swiss government bond yield sits at just 0.6149%, according to LSEG.
Like the yen, the Swiss franc has fallen, although not to the same extent. The franc recently hit its lowest levels since mid-2025 against the dollar and the euro.
"We think the Swiss franc overall will remain strong. We don't think that the Swiss franc will lose a significant percentage of its value," Jung said.

Meanwhile, there is always the possibility of a shock in the near future that could cause the Swiss franc to appreciate, with investors buying the currency as a safe haven, while many others would seek a swift exit from risky carry trades funded in francs, Farquet said.
